# Part 1: Warm-up with one dataset

## Generate data with a constant hazard

```{r}
set.seed(2026)   
source("R/functions.R")
gen_data <- function(n, hr, rate_old, cens_rate) {
  group   <- rep(c("old", "new"), each = n)
  rate    <- ifelse(group == "old", rate_old, rate_old * hr)
  t_event <- rexp(2 * n, rate)        
  t_cens  <- rexp(2 * n, cens_rate)    # time at which each patient is lost to follow-up
  data.frame(
    group = group,
    time  = pmin(t_event, t_cens),             # record whichever comes first
    event = as.integer(t_event <= t_cens)      # 1 = event observed, 0 = censored
  )
}

d <- gen_data(n = 300, hr = 0.7, rate_old = 0.05, cens_rate = 0.02)
head(d)
mean(d$event == 0)   # proportion censored
```

**Q1. Why the exponential distribution for event times?**\
It means a constant hazard: the risk of an event is the same at every moment. That gives the simplest proportional-hazards baseline. For delayed effects I would use a piecewise hazard instead.

**Q3. Why is censoring independent of the event time?**\
It assumes dropout is unrelated to prognosis (non-informative censoring), which Cox and log-rank rely on. If sicker patients dropped out earlier, the results would be biased.

**`rexp(n, rate)`**\
It draws `n` random event times, one per patient, from an exponential distribution. A larger `rate` (hazard) gives shorter times.

**Mean time = 1 / hazard**\
A hazard of 0.05 per month means one event every 20 months on average. Individual times vary a lot around that average.

## Cox model and log-rank test

```{r}
library(survival)   # survival analysis package, comes with R

# make "old" the reference group, so the HR is new vs old
d$group <- factor(d$group, levels = c("old", "new"))
# Cox model: estimates one hazard ratio
fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ group, data = d)
summary(fit_cox)

# log-rank test: do the two survival curves differ?
fit_lr <- survdiff(Surv(time, event) ~ group, data = d)
fit_lr
```

**1. What does `Surv(time, event)` do?**\
It bundles follow-up time and event status (1 = event, 0 = censored) into one survival object, so the models know which observations are censored.

**2. How do you interpret the HR from the Cox model?**\
HR = 0.77 means the new group's hazard is 77% of the old group's at any time point (95% CI 0.63 to 0.94). It is a ratio of rates, not "23% fewer patients had an event".

**3. What is the difference between the Cox model and the log-rank test?**\
The log-rank test only tells you whether the curves differ (a p-value). The Cox model also gives the size of the effect (HR with a confidence interval). Under proportional hazards they give almost the same p-value.

**4. How does the log-rank test work?**\
At each event time it compares the observed number of events in each group with the number expected if the groups had the same hazard, then sums these differences into a chi-square statistic.

**5. Why did you set `levels = c("old", "new")`?**\
So "old" is the reference group and the HR is new vs old. Without it, R sorts alphabetically and the HR would be inverted (about 1.3 instead of 0.77).

**6. What assumption do both methods rely on?**\
Proportional hazards: the hazard ratio is constant over time. If it changes (delayed effect, crossing curves), the HR and log-rank test can be misleading, which is exactly what this simulation tests.

## Kaplan-Meier curves

```{r}
# Kaplan-Meier estimate: proportion event-free over time, one curve per group
fit_km <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ group, data = d)

plot(fit_km,
     col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),   # order follows the factor: old, new
     lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Months",
     ylab = "Proportion event-free")

legend("topright", legend = c("old", "new"),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2)
```

# Part 2: Three hazard scenarios

## Simulated data and Kaplan-Meier curves

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
d_ph <- gen_data2(300, 0.05, hr1 = 0.7, hr2 = 0.7, tau = 6, cens_rate = 0.02) #proportional
d_delay <- gen_data2(300, 0.05, hr1 = 1.0, hr2 = 0.5, tau = 6, cens_rate = 0.02)  # delayed effect
d_cross <- gen_data2(300, 0.05, hr1 = 1.5, hr2 = 0.5, tau = 6, cens_rate = 0.02)  # crossing curves

plot_km <- function(d, title) {
  fit <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ group, data = d)
  plot(fit, col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2,
       xlab = "Months", ylab = "Proportion event-free", main = title)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))   # three plots side by side
plot_km(d_ph,    "Proportional")
plot_km(d_delay, "Delayed effect")
plot_km(d_cross, "Crossing curves")
```

## Cox and log-rank on one dataset per scenario

```{r}
rbind(proportional = run_methods(d_ph),
      delayed      = run_methods(d_delay),
      crossing     = run_methods(d_cross))
```

## Power of Cox and log-rank (200 replications)

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

sim_power <- function(nsim, hr1, hr2) {
  res <- replicate(nsim, {
    d <- gen_data2(300, 0.05, hr1 = hr1, hr2 = hr2, tau = 6, cens_rate = 0.02)
    run_methods(d)   # returns HR, p_cox, p_logrank
  })
  # res has 3 rows (HR, p_cox, p_logrank) and nsim columns, one per repetition
  c(mean_HR       = mean(res["HR", ]),
    power_cox     = mean(res["p_cox", ] < 0.05),
    power_logrank = mean(res["p_logrank", ] < 0.05))
}

rbind(proportional = sim_power(200, 0.7, 0.7),
      delayed      = sim_power(200, 1.0, 0.5),
      crossing     = sim_power(200, 1.5, 0.5))
```

## RMST difference on one dataset per scenario

```{r}
rmst_diff(d_ph)
rmst_diff(d_delay)
rmst_diff(d_cross)
```

## True RMST difference

```{r}
old <- rmst_true(0.05, 0.05)
c(proportional = rmst_true(0.035, 0.035) - old,
  delayed      = rmst_true(0.05, 0.025)  - old,
  crossing     = rmst_true(0.075, 0.025) - old)
```

## Bias and rejection rates of the three methods (200 replications)

```{r}
sim_summary <- function(nsim, hr1, hr2) {
  res <- replicate(nsim, {
    d <- gen_data2(300, 0.05, hr1 = hr1, hr2 = hr2, tau = 6, cens_rate = 0.02)
    c(run_methods(d), rmst_diff(d))   # HR, p_cox, p_logrank, rmst_diff, p_rmst
  })
  # true RMST difference for this scenario (no random numbers involved)
  truth <- rmst_true(0.05 * hr1, 0.05 * hr2) - rmst_true(0.05, 0.05)
  c(true_rmst_diff = truth,
    mean_rmst_diff = mean(res["rmst_diff", ]),           # average of the 200 estimates
    bias           = mean(res["rmst_diff", ]) - truth,   # average estimate minus truth
    reject_cox     = mean(res["p_cox", ] < 0.05),
    reject_logrank = mean(res["p_logrank", ] < 0.05),
    reject_rmst    = mean(res["p_rmst", ] < 0.05))
}

set.seed(2026)
out <- rbind(null         = sim_summary(200, 1.0, 1.0),
             proportional = sim_summary(200, 0.7, 0.7),
             delayed      = sim_summary(200, 1.0, 0.5),
             crossing     = sim_summary(200, 1.5, 0.5))
round(out, 3)
```

## Censoring rate for a target share of censored patients

```{r}
cens_rate_for(0.2)   # 0.0125
cens_rate_for(0.5)   # 0.05

# check: simulate a very large trial and measure the share censored
check_cens <- function(target, hr1, hr2) {
  d <- gen_data2(50000, 0.05, hr1, hr2, tau = 6, cens_rate = cens_rate_for(target))
  mean(d$event == 0)
}
check_cens(0.2, 1.0, 1.0)   # null
check_cens(0.2, 0.7, 0.7)   # proportional
check_cens(0.2, 1.0, 0.5)   # delayed
check_cens(0.2, 1.5, 0.5)   # crossing
```

# Part 3: Full simulation results (24 scenarios, 1000 replications)

## Summary of the results

**Results summary** (1000 replications per scenario; `mcse_*` is the Monte Carlo standard error)

1.  **Type I error (null rows):** the reject rates of all three methods are close to the nominal 5%, so none of them raises false alarms.

2.  **Accuracy of RMST:** bias is the mean estimate minus the true value, and `mcse_bias` is the Monte Carlo SE of that mean. As a rule of thumb, a bias is not clearly different from zero when \|bias\| \< 2 × `mcse_bias`. For example, in crossing with censoring 0.5 and n = 600, the true RMST difference is 0.097849 and the mean estimate is 0.097387, so bias = −0.00046. This is far smaller than `mcse_bias` = 0.019001, so the estimate is not clearly biased.

3.  **Proportional and delayed effects:** Cox and log-rank detect the effect more often than RMST (delayed, censoring 0.2, n = 300: 0.997 vs 0.727).

4.  **Crossing curves:** the power of Cox and log-rank rises with n (0.331, 0.75, 0.965 at censoring 0.2), while RMST stays near 5% because the true 24-month RMST difference is tiny (0.097849). The methods answer different questions: "do the hazards differ?" versus "how many months are gained by month 24?"

5.  **Heavy censoring:** fewer observed events lower the power of Cox and log-rank (crossing, censoring 0.5, n = 600: 0.143).

6.  **Noise:** differences smaller than about 2 × `mcse` are likely random.

7.  **Limitation:** the results apply only to this design (hazard switch at month 6, RMST horizon of 24 months, baseline rate 0.05). No method is best everywhere.

## Reshape the results for plotting

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

results <- read.csv("results2.csv")

# Reshape to long format: one row per scenario x method
power_long <- results |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(reject_cox, reject_logrank, reject_rmst),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "reject"
  )

head(power_long)
```

## Power by method, scenario, censoring and sample size

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(power_long, aes(x = n, y = reject, colour = method)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  # Dashed line marks the 5% significance level
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  # Rows = censoring level, columns = scenario
  facet_grid(cens ~ shape) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 300, 600)) +
  labs(x = "Sample size per group", y = "Reject rate")
```

**Figure: reject rate by method, scenario, censoring level and sample size** (dashed line = 5% significance level)

1.  **Null scenario:** all three methods stay close to the dashed 5% line at every sample size and censoring level, so none of them raises false alarms.

2.  **Proportional and delayed effects:** the reject rate rises with sample size for all methods. Cox and log-rank are above RMST, and the gap is largest in the delayed scenario (censoring 0.2, n = 300: 0.997 vs 0.727).

3.  **Crossing curves:** the reject rate of Cox and log-rank rises with sample size at censoring 0.2 (0.331, 0.75, 0.965), while RMST stays near 5% because the true 24-month RMST difference is tiny (0.097849).

4.  **Heavy censoring:** the censoring 0.5 row is lower than the censoring 0.2 row, because fewer observed events mean less information, not because the methods become biased.

5.  **Cox and log-rank** give almost identical results, so their lines overlap.

## True survival curves of the three scenarios

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# Grid of time points (months)
t_grid <- seq(0, 60, by = 0.5)

# True survival curves for each non-null scenario
curve_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("proportional", "delayed", "crossing"), function(s) {
  hr <- hr_table[[s]]
  rbind(
    data.frame(shape = s, group = "old", t = t_grid, surv = S(t_grid, 0.05, 0.05)),
    data.frame(shape = s, group = "new", t = t_grid,
               surv = S(t_grid, 0.05 * hr[1], 0.05 * hr[2]))
  )
}))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(x = t, y = surv, colour = group)) +
  geom_line() +
  # Dotted line = hazard switch (month 6), dashed line = RMST horizon (month 24)
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 24, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ shape) +
  labs(x = "Months", y = "Survival probability")
```

**Figure: true survival curves of the old and new treatment in the three non-null scenarios.** The dotted line marks the hazard switch (month 6) and the dashed line marks the RMST horizon (month 24).

1.  **Proportional:** new stays above old from the start, and the gap widens gradually.

2.  **Delayed effect:** the two curves coincide until month 6, then new separates from old.

3.  **Crossing:** new is below old early on, the curves cross shortly after month 6, and new is above old afterwards.

4.  **RMST:** the area under each curve up to month 24. In the crossing scenario, the area lost before the crossing roughly cancels the area gained after it, so the true 24-month RMST difference is only 0.097849, even though the hazards clearly differ.
